opus-5.5.text:
I usually start by asking what the benchmark is actually a proxy for. A benchmark is never the goal in itself. It's a stand-in for some capability we care about, so the first question is whether moving that number means the system can do something new in the real world, or just that it's gotten better at the test.

A few signals help me judge that. One is where we are on the curve. Early on, when models are scoring 30 or 40 percent, gains usually reflect real progress. Once you're in the high 90s, you have to ask whether the remaining errors are meaningful or just label noise and ambiguous questions. At that stage, an extra half a percent can be nothing more than overfitting to the quirks of the dataset, especially once the whole community has been tuning against the same test set for years.

Another is how the improvement was achieved. If it comes from a new idea that generalizes, like a better way of training or a capability that also lifts performance on other tasks, that's exciting. If it comes from benchmark-specific tricks, or brute-force compute that gets you a tiny gain, it's much less interesting. A good check is to change the setting a little: rephrase the questions, swap in a fresh task from the same domain, and see whether the improvement survives.

Then there's the question of what failures remain and whether they matter. In something like software engineering, the benchmark has to reflect real work, such as understanding a large codebase and producing a fix that actually passes tests. That's part of why we built SWE-bench around real GitHub issues. When a model improves on a task like that, it's easier to believe the gain translates, and the headroom tells you there's still a lot worth pursuing.

So my rule of thumb is that an improvement is worth chasing if it's tied to a capability people care about, if it holds up outside the exact test, and if it teaches you something you can carry over to other problems. And when a benchmark stops giving you that, when it's saturated or being gamed, the most valuable move is often not to squeeze out another point but to build a better benchmark.

r001.rationale: It says gains at 30–40% usually reflect real progress, while a half-point gain near the high 90s may reflect noise or overfitting.

r002.rationale: It recommends building a better benchmark when the current one is saturated or being gamed.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because benchmarks are both the thing that drives progress in this field and the thing that most often misleads it.

The way I try to think about it is: a benchmark is a proxy. It's never the thing we actually care about. We care about whether a model can help someone write software, or reason through a hard scientific problem, or navigate a website to accomplish a task. The benchmark is a compressed, measurable stand-in for that. So the first question I ask is, how much daylight is there between the proxy and the real capability? If a benchmark is saturated, or if the gap between the test and the actual use case has grown wide, then squeezing out another two points doesn't tell you much. It usually tells you more about the training data than about the model.

A few signals I look for. One, does the improvement transfer? If you get better on one coding benchmark and it shows up on a different one you didn't optimize for, that's meaningful. If it only shows up on the one you targeted, you should be suspicious. Two, does the improvement change what someone would actually do with the system? There's a threshold effect in a lot of these tasks. Going from 30 percent to 40 percent on something like resolving real GitHub issues might not change anything in practice. Going from 70 to 85 might mean a developer actually starts trusting the tool. The same delta can be worthless in one regime and transformative in another. Three, how was the number achieved? Did it come from a genuinely new idea, better data, more compute, or did it come from something closer to contamination or test-set overfitting? The first few are worth pursuing. The last one is noise, and sometimes worse than noise because it corrupts the signal for everyone else.

The other thing I'd say is that the right benchmarks are the ones that are hard to game because they're close to reality. When we built SWE-bench, the whole motivation was that existing coding evaluations were these small, self-contained puzzles, and models were getting good at puzzles without getting good at working in a real codebase. So we tried to make the benchmark as close as possible to the actual job. When you do that, improvements become much more trustworthy, because there's less room between the metric and the thing you want.

So my short answer is: an improvement is worth pursuing if it reflects a real capability change, if it transfers, and if it moves the system across a threshold that matters to the people who'd use it. If it's just moving a number on a leaderboard, I'd rather spend the effort building a better benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says small gains on a saturated benchmark may not tell us much, but it does not clearly state that large gains are clearer signals of progress in that setting.

r002.rationale: It recommends spending effort building a better benchmark when gains are merely moving a leaderboard number, and explains that benchmarks should be closer to real use.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what is the benchmark actually measuring, and why do we care about that capability? A higher score is useful if it tells us the system can do something meaningful that it couldn’t do before. But the score itself shouldn’t become the goal.

I’d also look at the errors. If an improvement means the model is handling a genuinely different class of problems, that’s interesting—even if the aggregate gain is small. If it mostly comes from tuning to the quirks of a particular dataset, I’m less excited.

And then there’s the cost. How much additional data or computation did it take? Does the improvement hold up on new examples? For me, it’s worth pursuing when it either gives us a useful capability or teaches us something about how to build better systems.

r001.rationale: The response discusses meaningful capability gains and dataset quirks, but does not say that large gains are clearer signals than small gains near benchmark saturation.

r002.rationale: The response does not recommend moving attention to a new challenge when a benchmark becomes saturated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is: what is the benchmark actually measuring? Ideally, an improvement tells us that the model has acquired some capability we care about, rather than just gotten better at the particular test.

So I’d look at the errors. If you go from 80 to 85 percent, are you solving a new class of problems, or are you fixing a few quirks in the dataset? And does that improvement carry over when you change the wording or move to a slightly different setting?

There’s also the cost. If you need ten times as much computation for a very small gain, that might be less interesting than a method that gets the same performance with much less data. For me, the number is a starting point. What makes it worth pursuing is understanding what changed and why that change matters.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts meaningful capability gains with dataset quirks and discusses an 80-to-85 percent improvement, but it does not say that large gains are clearer progress signals when models are near benchmark saturation.
